items.text: Autistic burnout and clinical depression can look similar. But they have different roots — and treating burnout like depression can actively make it worse. The distinction matters.
items.rationale: Names a consequential misconception and states the stakes clearly. The AASPIRE 2026 study gives this a live research peg. Avoids prescribing treatment while making the clinical risk concrete.
items.sensitivity_flag: "Can actively make it worse" is directional about treatment — defensible via the AASPIRE study but should not appear alongside any implied instruction to avoid specific clinical interventions.

items.text: The autistic community has been saying burnout and depression are different for years. A 2026 study just gave it research legs. Community knowledge is knowledge.
items.rationale: Credits the community as the original source rather than positioning research as the revelation. The 2026 AASPIRE citation (379 participants, Autism journal) anchors the specific claim defensibly.
items.sensitivity_flag: Specific study claim (AASPIRE, 379 participants) drawn from briefing — confirm publication and participant count directly before posting.

items.text: Non-autistic people run most social interactions on autopilot. Many autistic people are manually piloting every exchange. Same destination. Completely different fuel burn.
items.rationale: Translates masking's cognitive cost into a frame immediately legible to people who don't experience it. 'Fuel burn' makes cumulative depletion visceral without clinical language.

items.text: Masking isn't pretending to be someone else. It's running a learned script in real time, every conversation. The exhaustion people on the outside don't see is the evidence.
items.rationale: Shifts masking from a performance framing to a cognitive-load framing — which is both more accurate and more compassionate. The last sentence validates the hidden effort without sentimentality.

items.text: Remote work was the best accommodation many neurodivergent workers ever had. Nobody called it that at the time. What are we actually asking people to give up with RTO mandates?
items.rationale: The question form invites genuine reflection rather than performing outrage. 'Nobody called it that' does the reframe economically. Anchored in a live policy moment with real community stakes.

items.text: What looks like 'won't' in a PDAer is usually a nervous system in threat mode — not a choice, not manipulation. Strategies that assume choice tend to make it worse.
items.rationale: The won't-vs-can't reframe is the single most consequential shift in PDA understanding. 'PDAer' is correct identity-first usage. 'Tend to' hedges the outcome claim appropriately.

items.text: Late diagnosis can arrive as two things at once: 'that explains everything' and 'I'm mourning the years I didn't have this.' Both are real. You don't have to pick one.
items.rationale: Names the dual experience late-diagnosed people describe constantly but rarely see articulated together. Direct second-person feels like recognition, not clinical description.

items.text: Getting a late autism diagnosis doesn't just explain the past. It rewrites it. That rewrite takes time. It's supposed to.
items.rationale: Four short sentences, each doing distinct work. The last one is the validation — reframing the slowness of integration as correct rather than a personal failure. Tight and quotable.

items.text: If you have ADHD and autism, your brain might crave novelty to feel alive and need routine to feel safe — at the same time. That's not a contradiction. That's the AuDHD experience.
items.rationale: Names the internal paradox precisely. 'Might' avoids speaking for everyone. The final sentence offers belonging rather than a fix, which is exactly what this angle calls for.

items.text: The test for any ADHD productivity system isn't 'does it work on a good day.' It's 'can I actually use it on my worst one.' Complex systems consume executive function. They don't save it.
items.rationale: Flips standard productivity advice in a way that is both actionable and validating. The last two sentences carry the core insight: a system that requires capacity to operate is not a system.

items.text: Co-regulation isn't something you switch on when your PDA kid is in meltdown. It's something you've already been building — through your own regulation, the relationship, the small moments before the hard ones.
items.rationale: Meets parents at the point of guilt and reframes the problem without dismissing the difficulty. The list at the end is concrete without being prescriptive.

items.text: In a heightened moment with a PDA child, the work of co-regulation was done before it was needed. That's not failure when it doesn't appear on demand. That's how nervous system safety actually gets built.
items.rationale: Companion to the co-regulation reframe — speaks to the parent's in-the-moment experience of 'I'm failing right now.' Converts that failure framing into a process framing, which is both accurate and compassionate.
